p.src: Now among Cao Cao’s officers, apart from Zhang Liao, only Xu Huang was close to Yunzhang, though all the others respected and admired him; Cai Yang alone resented Lord Guan, and when he heard that Guan had departed that day, he wanted to stop him and give chase. Cao Cao said, “He does not forget his former lord, and his coming and going are open and honorable. He is a true man of character. You should all follow his example.” He rebuked Cai Yang and sent him away, forbidding him to pursue Guan. Cheng Yu said, “The Chancellor treated Guan with the greatest generosity, yet now he has left without taking his leave, presuming to offend Your Excellency with a few disorderly words on a scrap of paper. His offense is grave. If we let him return to Yuan Shao, it will be like giving wings to a tiger. Better to pursue and kill him, thereby ending any future danger.” Cao Cao said, “I gave him my word long ago. How could I break faith? Each of us serves his own lord. Do not pursue him.” Then he said to Zhang Liao, “Yunzhang sealed up the gold and hung up his seal. Riches could not sway his heart, nor rank and emolument alter his purpose. I deeply respect such a man. He cannot have gone far. I will show him one final kindness and strengthen our bond. Ride ahead and ask him to wait. I shall see him off and present him with traveling expenses and a campaign robe as a remembrance for the future.” Zhang Liao accepted the order and rode ahead alone. Cao Cao followed with several dozen riders.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Red Hare ridden by Yunzhang could cover a thousand li in a day and ordinarily could not have been overtaken; but because he wished to escort the carriages, he dared not give the horse its head and rode slowly with a restrained rein. Suddenly he heard someone behind him cry, “Yunzhang, slow your pace!” Looking back, he saw Zhang Liao galloping toward him. Lord Guan ordered the carriage attendants to keep hurrying along the main road; then he himself reined in Red Hare, steadied the Green Dragon blade, and asked, “Wenyuan, have you come to pursue me and take me back?” Zhang Liao replied, “No. The Chancellor learned that you were setting out on a long journey and wishes to see you off. He sent me ahead especially to ask Your Honor to wait. He has no other intention.” Lord Guan said, “Even if the Chancellor’s armored cavalry comes, I am ready to fight them to the death!” He halted his horse upon the bridge and watched. He saw Cao Cao galloping toward him with several dozen riders; behind him rode Xu Chu, Xu Huang, Yu Jin, Li Dian, and the others.

p.src: Seeing Lord Guan mounted on the bridge with his blade held crosswise, Cao Cao ordered his generals to rein in and form ranks on either side. Only when Lord Guan saw that none of them held a weapon did he feel reassured. Cao Cao said, “Yunzhang, why do you travel with such haste?” Lord Guan inclined himself in the saddle and replied, “I informed the Chancellor before that my former lord is now north of the Yellow River, so I cannot but hasten to him. I called at your residence several times but was unable to obtain an audience, so I left a letter of farewell, sealed the gold, hung up my seal, and returned them to the Chancellor. I trust the Chancellor will not forget his former words.” Cao Cao said, “I seek to win the trust of all under Heaven. How could I go back on what I said before? Fearing that you might lack provisions on your journey, I have specially prepared traveling funds to see you on your way.” One officer extended a tray of gold from horseback. Lord Guan said, “I have repeatedly received your generous gifts and still have ample funds. Keep this gold to reward your officers and men.” Cao Cao said, “This is merely a small recompense for one part in ten thousand of your great service. Why refuse it?” Lord Guan replied, “My trifling service is scarcely worth mentioning.” Cao Cao laughed and said, “Yunzhang is a righteous hero of the realm. I regret that my fortune is too slight to keep you with me. Accept this brocade robe as a small token of my regard.” He ordered an officer to dismount and bring the robe forward in both hands. Fearing some treachery, Yunzhang dared not dismount. With the tip of his Green Dragon blade he lifted the brocade robe and draped it over himself, then reined his horse around and thanked Cao Cao, saying, “I am grateful to the Chancellor for this robe. We shall meet again another day.” He descended from the bridge and headed north. Xu Chu said, “This man is intolerably discourteous. Why not seize him?” Cao Cao replied, “He is alone with a single horse, while we number several dozen. How could he fail to be suspicious? My word has been given. We must not pursue him.” Cao Cao led his generals back to the city, sighing and thinking of Yunzhang throughout the journey.

p.src: We leave Cao Cao to make his return. As for Lord Guan, he hurried after the carriages, but though he traveled some thirty li, they were nowhere to be seen. Alarmed, Yunzhang spurred his horse and searched in every direction. Suddenly a man on a hilltop cried out, “General Guan, wait!” Yunzhang looked up and saw a young man in a yellow headscarf and brocade garments, carrying a spear astride a horse, with a severed head hanging beneath its neck. Leading over a hundred foot soldiers, he came racing forward. Lord Guan asked, “Who are you?” The young man cast down his spear, dismounted, and prostrated himself upon the ground. Suspecting a trick, Yunzhang held his horse in check and kept his blade ready as he asked, “Good warrior, state your name.” He replied, “I am a native of Xiangyang; my surname is Liao, my given name Hua, and my courtesy name Yuanjian. In the chaos of these times I became a wanderer, gathered more than five hundred followers, and lived by plunder. Just now my companion Du Yuan went down the mountain on patrol and mistakenly abducted the two ladies and brought them up here. I questioned their attendants and learned that they were the wives of Imperial Uncle Liu of the Great Han. When I also heard that you were escorting them nearby, I immediately sought to bring them down the mountain. Du Yuan spoke insolently, so I killed him. I now present his head to you and beg forgiveness.” Lord Guan asked, “Where are the two ladies?” Liao Hua replied, “They are now on the mountain.” Lord Guan ordered that they be brought down at once. Before long, more than a hundred men came escorting the carriages. Lord Guan dismounted, rested his blade, and stood before the carriage with hands respectfully folded, asking, “Were you frightened, my sisters-in-law?” The two ladies said, “Had General Liao not protected us, Du Yuan would already have dishonored us.” Lord Guan asked the attendants, “How did Liao Hua rescue the ladies?” The attendants replied, “After Du Yuan abducted them to the mountain, he proposed that he and Liao Hua should each take one as a wife. When Liao Hua asked about their origins, he treated them with the greatest reverence; but Du Yuan would not agree, so Liao Hua killed him.” On hearing this, Lord Guan bowed and thanked Liao Hua. Liao Hua wished to send some of his men along as Lord Guan’s escort. Lord Guan reflected that the man was, after all, a remnant of the Yellow Turbans and not yet fit to be his companion, so he thanked him and declined. Liao Hua again bowed and offered gold and silk, but Lord Guan refused these as well. Liao Hua bowed farewell, then led his companions away into the mountain valleys.

p.src: Yunzhang told his two sisters-in-law how Cao Cao had given him the robe, then urged the carriages onward. At nightfall, they sought lodging at a country estate. The master of the estate, whose beard and hair were entirely white, came out to greet them and asked, “General, what is your name? Lord Guan saluted and said, “I am Guan, younger brother of Liu Xuande.” The old man said, “Can you be Lord Guan, who slew Yan Liang and Wen Chou?” Lord Guan replied, “I am.” Overjoyed, the old man invited him into the estate. Lord Guan said, “There are also two ladies in the carriages.” The old man at once called his wife and daughters out to welcome them. When the two ladies entered the thatched hall, Lord Guan stood respectfully at their side with his hands folded. The old man invited him to sit, but Lord Guan said, “With my honored sisters-in-law seated above me, how could I dare take a seat?” The old man then had his wife and daughters invite the two ladies into the inner chambers and attend to them, while he himself entertained Lord Guan in the thatched hall. Lord Guan asked the old man’s name. The old man said, “My surname is Hu and my given name Hua. During Emperor Huan’s reign I served as a Gentleman Consultant, but I retired from office and returned to my native village. I have a son named Hu Ban, who now serves as an assistant officer under Wang Zhi, Governor of Xingyang. If you pass that way, General, I have a letter I would ask you to deliver to my son.” Lord Guan agreed.

p.src: After breakfast the next day, Guan Yu invited his two sisters-in-law into the carriage, took Hu Hua's letter, bade him farewell, and set out on the road to Luoyang. Ahead lay a pass called Dongling Pass. The commander guarding it was Kong Xiu, who held the earthen ridge with five hundred soldiers. That day, as Guan Yu escorted the carriages up the ridge, soldiers reported his arrival to Kong Xiu, who came out of the pass to meet him. Guan Yu dismounted and exchanged courtesies with Kong Xiu. Kong Xiu asked, “Where are you going, General?” Guan Yu replied, “I have taken leave of the Prime Minister and am going expressly to Hebei to seek my elder brother.” Kong Xiu said, “Yuan Shao of Hebei is the Prime Minister's sworn enemy; surely you have a travel warrant from the Prime Minister.” Guan Yu replied, “My departure was so hurried that I had no time to obtain one.” Kong Xiu said, “Since you have no warrant, I must send someone to report to the Prime Minister before I can let you pass.” Guan Yu said, “By the time your report returns, my journey will have been delayed.” Kong Xiu replied, “The law binds me; I have no choice.” Guan Yu said, “Will you not let me through the pass?” Kong Xiu said, “If you wish to pass, leave the women and attendants behind as hostages.” Guan Yu flew into a rage, raised his blade, and moved to kill Kong Xiu. Kong Xiu retreated inside the pass, beat the drum to muster his troops, donned his armor, mounted, and charged down, shouting, “Do you dare try to pass?” Guan Yu ordered the carriages to withdraw, spurred his horse forward with blade in hand, and without another word rode straight at Kong Xiu. Kong Xiu leveled his spear and met him. Their horses crossed, and in a single exchange the steel blade flashed and Kong Xiu's corpse fell beneath his horse. The soldiers immediately fled. Guan Yu called, “Soldiers, do not flee. I killed Kong Xiu only because I had no choice; this has nothing to do with you. Tell Prime Minister Cao on my behalf that Kong Xiu sought to harm me, and therefore I killed him.” All the soldiers bowed before his horse.

p.src: Guan Yu then had the two ladies' carriages brought through the pass and set out toward Luoyang. Soldiers had already reported the news to Han Fu, Governor of Luoyang. Han Fu hurriedly assembled his officers to deliberate. His subordinate officer Meng Tan said, “Since he has no warrant from the Prime Minister, he is traveling without authorization; if we do not stop him, we shall surely be held responsible.” Han Fu said, “Guan Yu is fierce and valiant; both Yan Liang and Wen Chou were slain by him. We cannot oppose him by force; we must capture him by stratagem.” Meng Tan said, “I have a plan. First barricade the pass with chevaux-de-frise. When he arrives, I shall lead troops against him, feign defeat, and lure him into pursuit; then you can shoot him from concealment. Once Guan falls from his horse, we can seize him and send him under guard to Xudu, and we shall surely receive a rich reward.” When their preparations were settled, someone reported that Guan Yu's carriages had arrived. Han Fu drew his bow and nocked an arrow, led out a thousand horse and foot, arrayed them at the pass, and demanded, “Who comes there?” Guan Yu inclined himself in the saddle and said, “I am Guan, Lord of Hanshou; I ask leave to pass through.” Han Fu asked, “Have you a warrant from Prime Minister Cao?” Guan Yu replied, “Pressing affairs prevented me from obtaining one.” Han Fu said, “By the Prime Minister's august command, I guard this place expressly to question spies passing to and fro. Anyone without a warrant is a fugitive.” Guan Yu said angrily, “Kong Xiu of Dongling has already fallen to my blade. Do you too seek death?” Han Fu cried, “Who will seize him for me?” Meng Tan rode out, whirling his twin sabers, and charged at Guan Yu. Guan Yu ordered the carriages back and spurred forward to meet him. Before three exchanges had passed, Meng Tan wheeled his horse and fled. Guan Yu pursued him. Meng Tan had meant only to lure Guan Yu on, but Guan Yu's horse was swifter than he expected and soon overtook him; with one stroke Guan cut him in two. As Guan Yu reined about, Han Fu stepped from beside the gate and loosed an arrow with all his strength, striking Guan in the left arm. Guan Yu pulled the arrow out with his teeth; blood streamed unchecked, yet he galloped straight at Han Fu and scattered the troops. Han Fu could not dodge in time; Guan Yu's arm rose and his blade fell, cleaving him from head through shoulder and striking him beneath his horse; then Guan scattered the remaining soldiers and returned to protect the carriages.

p.src: Guan Yu tore silk to bind his arrow wound. Fearing ambush on the road, he dared not linger and traveled through the night toward Sishui Pass. The commander of the pass was a man of Bingzhou named Bian Xi, skilled in wielding the meteor hammer; originally a remnant of the Yellow Turban rebels, he had later joined Cao Cao and been assigned to guard the pass. On hearing that Guan Yu was approaching, he devised a scheme. At Zhenguo Temple before the pass, he concealed more than two hundred axemen, intending to lure Guan Yu into the temple and, at the signal of a struck cup, have him murdered. His arrangements complete, he went out of the pass to welcome Guan Yu. Seeing Bian Xi come to meet him, Guan Yu dismounted to greet him. Bian Xi said, “Your fame shakes the realm, General; who does not revere you? Now that you are returning to the Imperial Uncle, your loyalty and honor are plain to see!” Guan Yu told him how he had slain Kong Xiu and Han Fu. Bian Xi said, “You were right to kill them, General. When I see the Prime Minister, I shall explain the circumstances on your behalf.” Guan Yu was delighted. They mounted together, passed through Sishui Pass, and dismounted before Zhenguo Temple. The monks rang the bell and came out to welcome them. Zhenguo Temple was in fact an imperial incense sanctuary founded under Emperor Ming of Han, and housed more than thirty monks. Among them was one monk from Guan Yu's own homeland, whose religious name was Pujing. Pujing already knew what was intended. He stepped forward, saluted Guan Yu, and asked, “How many years has it been since you left Pudong, General?” Guan Yu replied, “Nearly twenty years.” Pujing asked, “Do you still recognize this poor monk?” Guan Yu said, “I have been away from home for many years and do not recognize you.” Pujing said, “My family home and yours were separated by only one river.” Seeing Pujing speak of their ties as fellow townsmen, Bian Xi feared the secret might be divulged and rebuked him: “I mean to invite the general to a banquet. Why should a monk like you chatter so much?” Guan Yu said, “That is not so. When men from the same homeland meet, how could they not speak of old times?”

Guan Yu said, “I have been away from home for many years and do not recognize you.”
Pujing said, “My family home and yours were separated by only one river.”

Seeing Pujing speak of their ties as fellow townsmen, Bian Xi feared the secret might be divulged and rebuked him: “I mean to invite the general to a banquet. Why should a monk like you chatter so much?”
Guan Yu said, “That is not so.
When men from the same homeland meet, how could they not speak of old times?”

p.src: Pujing invited Guan Yu to the abbot's quarters for tea. Guan Yu said, “The two ladies are in the carriages; please serve them tea first.” Pujing ordered tea to be taken first to the ladies, and then invited Guan Yu into the abbot's quarters. Pujing raised the monastic knife at his waist with one hand and fixed Guan Yu with a meaningful look. Understanding his meaning, Guan Yu ordered his attendants to carry his blade and follow close behind. Bian Xi invited Guan Yu to the banquet in the Dharma Hall. Guan Yu asked, “Master Bian, do you invite me with good intentions, or with evil ones?” Before Bian Xi could answer, Guan Yu caught sight of axemen behind the wall hangings and roared at him, “I took you for an honorable man! How dare you do this?” Knowing the plot was exposed, Bian Xi shouted, “Men, strike!” Just as the men were about to attack, Guan Yu drew his sword and cut them down. Bian Xi fled down the hall and around the gallery; Guan Yu cast aside his sword, seized his great blade, and gave chase. Bian Xi secretly drew his flying hammer and hurled it at Guan Yu. Guan Yu knocked the hammer aside with his blade, pressed in, and split Bian Xi in two with one stroke; then he immediately turned back to see to his two sisters-in-law. Soldiers had already surrounded them, but on seeing Guan Yu approach, they fled in every direction. Guan Yu drove them off and thanked Pujing, saying, “But for you, Master, I would have been harmed by that villain.” Pujing said, “This place will no longer tolerate this poor monk. I shall gather my robe and bowl and wander elsewhere. We shall meet again someday. Take care, General.” Guan Yu thanked him, then escorted the carriages onward toward Xingyang.

p.src: Wang Zhi, Governor of Xingyang, was related to Han Fu by marriage; when he heard that Lord Guan had slain Han Fu, he plotted to murder him in secret and sent men to guard the pass. When Lord Guan arrived, Wang Zhi came out through the pass and welcomed him with a cheerful smile. Lord Guan told him of his journey to seek his brother. Wang Zhi said, “General, you have wearied yourself riding the roads, and the ladies are exhausted from traveling in the carriage. Pray enter the city and rest tonight at the posthouse. It will not be too late to resume your journey tomorrow.” Seeing how attentive Wang Zhi appeared, Lord Guan invited his two sisters-in-law to enter the city. Everything had been duly prepared at the posthouse. Wang Zhi invited Lord Guan to a banquet, but he declined to attend; so Wang Zhi had the feast sent to the posthouse. Wearied by the hardships of the road, Lord Guan asked his two sisters-in-law to retire in the main chamber after they had eaten; he ordered his attendants to rest as well and feed the horses well. Lord Guan likewise removed his armor and lay down to rest.

Lord Guan likewise removed his armor and lay down to rest.

p.src: Now Wang Zhi secretly summoned his aide Hu Ban and gave him these orders: “Guan has deserted the Chancellor and fled, and along the road he has slain governors and officers guarding the passes. His crime merits nothing less than death! His martial prowess makes him difficult to oppose. Tonight, muster one thousand troops to surround the posthouse, each man carrying a torch. At the third watch, set fire to it from every side at once; no matter who they are, burn them all to death! I myself will lead troops to support you.” Hu Ban accepted the order, mustered the soldiers, and secretly carried dry firewood and kindling to the entrance of the posthouse, there to await the appointed hour. Hu Ban thought, “I have long heard the name of Guan Yunchang, but I do not know what he looks like. Let me steal a glimpse of him.” He went into the posthouse and asked an attendant, “Where is General Guan?” The attendant replied, “He is the man reading in the main hall.” Hu Ban crept to the front of the hall and saw Lord Guan stroking his beard with his left hand as he leaned upon a table and read by lamplight. At the sight, Hu Ban involuntarily exclaimed, “Truly, he is a god among men!” Lord Guan asked who was there. Hu Ban entered, bowed, and said, “I am Hu Ban, an aide serving under the Governor of Xingyang.” Lord Guan said, “Are you perhaps the son of Hu Hua, who lives outside the capital of Xu?” Hu Ban replied, “I am.” Lord Guan called an attendant to take a letter from his baggage and hand it to Hu Ban. When Hu Ban had finished reading it, he exclaimed, “I nearly killed a loyal and worthy man by mistake!” He then warned him in secret: “Wang Zhi harbors wicked intentions and means to kill you, General. He has secretly ordered men to surround the posthouse on all sides and set it afire at the third watch. I shall go ahead now and open the city gate. Make ready at once, General, and leave the city.” Greatly alarmed, Lord Guan hastily donned his armor, took up his blade, and mounted. He asked his two sisters-in-law to enter their carriage, and the whole party left the posthouse, where indeed they saw soldiers waiting with torches in their hands. Lord Guan hurried to the city wall and found the gate already open. He urged the carriages and escort swiftly out of the city. Hu Ban went back and set the fire. Before Lord Guan had gone several li, torches blazed behind him as men and horses came in pursuit. At their head, Wang Zhi shouted, “Guan, halt!” Lord Guan reined in and cursed him: “You wretch! I bear you no enmity. Why did you order men to burn me alive?” Wang Zhi spurred his horse, leveled his spear, and charged straight at Lord Guan; but one sweep of Lord Guan’s blade cut him in two at the waist. His men and horses scattered. Lord Guan urged the carriages and escort onward at speed, all the while feeling deeply grateful to Hu Ban.

p.src: When they reached the border of Huazhou, someone reported their arrival to Liu Yan. Liu Yan led several dozen horsemen out from the town to welcome them. Lord Guan inclined his body from the saddle and said, “Governor, I trust you have been well since we parted!” Liu Yan asked, “Where are you bound now?” Lord Guan replied, “I have taken leave of the Chancellor and am going to seek my brother.” Liu Yan said, “Xuande is with Yuan Shao, who is the Chancellor’s enemy. How could the Chancellor permit you to go there?” Lord Guan said, “We settled this matter long ago.” Liu Yan said, “The pass at the Yellow River ferry is now held by Qin Qi, a subordinate of Xiahou Dun. I fear he will not allow you to pass.” Lord Guan asked, “What if you were to provide me with a boat, Governor?” Liu Yan replied, “Though I have boats, I dare not provide one.” Lord Guan said, “When I slew Yan Liang and Wen Chou, I helped deliver you from peril as well. Why, then, do you refuse me a single ferryboat today?” Liu Yan replied, “I only fear that if Xiahou Dun learns of it, he will surely punish me.” Realizing that Liu Yan was a man of no use, Lord Guan urged his carriages and escort onward by himself. When he reached the Yellow River ferry, Qin Qi led out troops and demanded, “Who goes there?” Lord Guan replied, “I am Guan, Lord of Hanshou.” Qin Qi asked, “Where are you going?” Lord Guan said, “I wish to go to Hebei and seek my elder brother, Liu Xuande. I have respectfully come to request passage across the river.” Qin Qi asked, “Where is the Chancellor’s written authorization?” Lord Guan replied, “I am not under the Chancellor’s command. What written authorization would I have?” Qin Qi said, “I hold this pass under General Xiahou’s orders. Even if you grew wings, you could not fly across!” Lord Guan grew furious and said, “Do you know what became of those who blocked my path along the road?” Qin Qi replied, “You have only slain obscure lesser officers. Do you dare kill me?” Lord Guan said angrily, “How do you compare with Yan Liang and Wen Chou?” Qin Qi flew into a rage, spurred his horse, raised his blade, and charged straight at Lord Guan. The two horses met, and in a single exchange Lord Guan’s blade rose and Qin Qi’s head fell. Lord Guan said, “The man who opposed me is dead. The rest of you need not flee in terror. Prepare a boat at once and ferry me across the river.” The soldiers hurriedly poled a boat to the bank. Lord Guan invited his two sisters-in-law aboard, and they crossed the river. Beyond the Yellow River lay Yuan Shao’s territory. Lord Guan had passed through five barriers and slain six officers. A later poet composed verses in praise of him:

p.src: As he rode, Lord Guan sighed to himself: “It was not my wish to kill men all along the road, but circumstances left me no choice. When Lord Cao learns of it, he will surely think me an ungrateful man.” As they traveled on, a lone rider suddenly appeared from the north and shouted, “Yunchang, wait!” Lord Guan reined in and looked: it was Sun Qian. Lord Guan asked, “What news has there been since we parted at Runan?” Sun Qian replied, “After you withdrew your troops, General, Liu Pi and Gong Du recaptured Runan; they sent me to Hebei to establish friendly relations with Yuan Shao and invite Xuande to join them in devising a plan to defeat Cao Cao. But unexpectedly, the officers and soldiers in Hebei are all jealous of one another. Tian Feng is still imprisoned; Ju Shou has been dismissed and is not employed; Shen Pei and Guo Tu each contend for power; and Yuan Shao is so suspicious and indecisive that he cannot hold to any course. Imperial Uncle Liu and I therefore discussed a plan for him first to escape. The Imperial Uncle has now gone to Runan to join Liu Pi. Fearing that you might not know and would instead go to Yuan Shao, where you might come to harm, he sent me especially to meet you on the road and guide you back. Fortunately, I have met you here. You should hasten to Runan and meet the Imperial Uncle.” Lord Guan told Sun Qian to pay his respects to the ladies. The ladies asked him for news. Sun Qian related everything in detail: “Yuan Shao twice sought to behead the Imperial Uncle, but fortunately he has now escaped and gone to Runan. My ladies, you may meet the Imperial Uncle there.” Both ladies covered their faces and wept. Following this advice, Lord Guan did not proceed into Hebei but headed straight for Runan. As they traveled, dust suddenly rose behind them, and a body of horsemen came in pursuit. At their head, Xiahou Dun shouted, “Guan, halt!” Indeed:
